# origincloud Provider

Manages Origin Cloud resources.

Credentials come from `credentials_file` when it is set, and otherwise from the environment, the first of: `ORIGINCLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN`, an access token; `ORIGINCLOUD_CREDENTIALS_FILE`, the path of a service account key's credentials file; a CI job's OIDC token, exchanged at the security token service for a `WORKLOAD` service account's access tokens (`ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE`, `ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN`, an HCP Terraform run's `TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN`, or a GitHub Actions job's token); the session the `origin` CLI stored at its last `origin id login`; on an instance that runs as a service account, the instance's metadata service.

With `impersonate_service_account`, or `ORIGINCLOUD_IMPERSONATE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`, the provider acts as that service account instead, exchanging the token of those credentials, a person's, at the security token service for the account's.

## Example Usage

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    origincloud = {
      source = "origincloudhq/origincloud"
    }
  }
}

# Credentials come from credentials_file, a service account key's
# credentials file, or else from the environment, such as
# ORIGINCLOUD_CREDENTIALS_FILE or a CI job's OIDC token.
provider "origincloud" {
  region           = "eu-central1"
  credentials_file = "/etc/origincloud/deployer.json"
}
```

## Names

A resource is identified by its full resource name,
`//{service}.origincloudapis.eu/{relative name}`, which is its `id`. An
argument that refers to another resource, in any service or project, takes
that resource's `id`, not its `name`, which is relative:

```terraform
resource "origincloud_pvs_snapshot" "data" {
  project       = "my-project-123"
  zone          = "eu-central1-az1"
  source_volume = origincloud_pvs_volume.data.id
}
```

An import takes either form. After v0.18, the state of a resource holds its
full name as `id`, and has no `urn`: Terraform upgrades an older state the
first time it reads it.

## Authentication with a service account key

Automation outside CI, such as a deployment server, acts as an `EXTERNAL`
service account with one of its keys. Create the key with
`origin iam service-accounts keys create`, or in the console: either saves
its credentials file, the only copy of the private key, to a file you name.
Give the provider the file's path, in `credentials_file` or in
`ORIGINCLOUD_CREDENTIALS_FILE`. The provider signs an assertion with the key,
exchanges it at the security token service for the account's access tokens,
and exchanges another before each token expires, so a long apply isn't cut
off. The audit log names the service account as the actor of every change.

```terraform
provider "origincloud" {
  credentials_file = "/etc/origincloud/deployer.json"
}
```

Keep the file like any secret: readable only by the user that runs
Terraform, and out of version control. Set, `credentials_file` comes before
every credential of the environment.

### Why there is no key resource

The API returns a key's private key once, in the answer to its creation.
A resource would have to keep it in the state, where everyone who can read
the state, or a backend that stores it, could act as the service account.
So the provider offers no resource that creates a key, and no data source
returns one: `origincloud_iam_service_account_key` and
`origincloud_iam_service_account_keys` read a key's public metadata only.
Create a key with the CLI or the console and hand the file to the system
that needs it. In CI, use no key at all: the job's OIDC token is exchanged
instead, as below.

## Authentication from CI

A CI job can act as a `WORKLOAD` service account with the OIDC token its CI
provider issues it, so that no secret is stored in the CI system. The
service account needs a federated credential that trusts the CI provider's
tokens, created with `origincloud_iam_federated_credential` or as
[Workload identity federation](https://docs.origincloud.eu/docs/iam/workload-identity-federation/)
on [docs.origincloud.eu](https://docs.origincloud.eu) describes, and the
roles the job needs.

The provider exchanges the job's token at the security token service,
`https://sts.origincloudapis.eu`, for the service account's access tokens.
It takes the first of:

1. The token in the file `ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE` names, read again at
   every exchange.
2. The token `ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN` holds. It can't be renewed, so it
   serves until it expires.
3. In an HCP Terraform run with dynamic credentials, the run's workload
   identity token, `TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN`, or the one of a tagged
   audience, `TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN_<TAG>`, when
   `ORIGINCLOUD_TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TAG` names the tag.
4. In a GitHub Actions job with `permissions: id-token: write`, the job's
   token, which the provider asks GitHub for, for the audience
   `https://sts.origincloudapis.eu`. `ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_AUDIENCE` asks for
   another audience, for a federated credential with an audience of its own.

`credentials_file`, `ORIGINCLOUD_ACCESS_TOKEN` and
`ORIGINCLOUD_CREDENTIALS_FILE` come first, so leave them unset in the job.
`ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_DISABLED=true` leaves the CI job's token out.

### GitHub Actions

The job needs `permissions: id-token: write`; nothing else is configured. See
[Authenticate from GitHub Actions without a secret](https://docs.origincloud.eu/docs/iam/github-actions/)
for the federated credential's conditions.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  apply:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      # Lets the job ask GitHub for its OIDC token, which the provider
      # exchanges for the service account's access tokens.
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform apply -auto-approve
```

### HCP Terraform

The workspace sets the environment variable
`TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_AUDIENCE` to `https://sts.origincloudapis.eu`, and
HCP Terraform then gives each plan and apply a token in
`TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN`, which the provider takes with no other
configuration. The federated credential uses the HCP Terraform preset: issuer
`https://app.terraform.io`, with a condition on `terraform_organization_id`,
and optionally on `terraform_workspace_id` and `terraform_run_phase`.

A workspace that asks for tokens for other audiences too tags this one, with
`TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_AUDIENCE_ORIGIN` for instance, and HCP Terraform
then sets `TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TOKEN_ORIGIN`. Set
`ORIGINCLOUD_TFC_WORKLOAD_IDENTITY_TAG=ORIGIN` as an environment variable of
the workspace, too, for the provider to read that token. With a tag set the
provider reads that token alone, and fails naming the variable if the run has
none.

### GitLab CI

The job names its ID token `ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN`, issued for
`https://sts.origincloudapis.eu`. See
[Authenticate from GitLab CI and other CI providers without a secret](https://docs.origincloud.eu/docs/iam/other-ci-providers/)
for the federated credential's conditions.

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
apply:
  image:
    name: hashicorp/terraform:1.16.2
    entrypoint: [""]
  # GitLab sets ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN to the job's OIDC token, issued for
  # the security token service, which the provider exchanges for the
  # service account's access tokens.
  id_tokens:
    ORIGINCLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN:
      aud: https://sts.origincloudapis.eu
  script:
    - terraform init
    - terraform apply -auto-approve
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
```

## Impersonating a service account

A person who runs Terraform on their own machine, logged in with
`origin id login`, can plan and apply with a service account's rights
rather than their own, such as the narrow ones of the account the pipeline
deploys with, without a key. Name the account by its full name in
`impersonate_service_account`, or in
`ORIGINCLOUD_IMPERSONATE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`:

```terraform
provider "origincloud" {
  impersonate_service_account = "//iam.origincloudapis.eu/organizations/acme/serviceAccounts/sa-deploy"
}
```

The provider takes the token of the credentials it finds, the CLI's
session, and exchanges it at the security token service,
`https://sts.origincloudapis.eu`, for the account's access token, and for a
new one before each expires: an account's token lives five minutes at
most. Every call then acts as the account. The audit log names the account
as the `actor` of each change and the person as its `acting_party`.

The person needs `iam.service_account.get_access_token` on the account:
the role `roles/iam.service-account-token-creator`, bound on the account,
or on its project or organization. Without it, the exchange is refused and
the plan fails, naming the account and the role, before the provider sends
any call: it never falls back to the person's own token. Only a person's
token can impersonate an account; a service account's can't impersonate
another.

Set, `impersonate_service_account` comes before the variable, and `""`
impersonates no one even when the variable is set, so an argument taken
from an empty Terraform variable runs with the person's own rights. The state holds no
token: the exchanged tokens stay in the provider's memory.

## Upgrading from v0.21

v0.22 removes the service account's client secret, which the API no longer
has:

- `ORIGINCLOUD_CLIENT_ID` and `ORIGINCLOUD_CLIENT_SECRET` are no longer read.
  Give the provider a key's credentials file instead, as above.
- `origincloud_iam_service_account` has no `client_id` or `client_secret`:
  remove references to them.
- The resource `origincloud_iam_service_account_key` is gone. A state that
  holds one fails to plan until it is removed from the state, which leaves
  the key in place: a `removed` block (Terraform 1.7 or later), or
  `terraform state rm`.

  ```terraform
  removed {
    from = origincloud_iam_service_account_key.deployer
    lifecycle {
      destroy = false
    }
  }
  ```

  Delete the key with the CLI or the console once nothing uses it.

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Optional

- `credentials_file` (String) The path of a service account key's credentials file, the JSON file `origin iam service-accounts keys create` or the console saved: the provider calls the API as that service account, exchanging an assertion signed with the key at the security token service for access tokens, and a new one before each expires. Set, it comes before every credential of the environment; left out, `ORIGINCLOUD_CREDENTIALS_FILE` names the file. The provider reads the file, and the state never holds the key: no resource or data source creates or returns one.
- `endpoint` (String) The URL every call goes to instead, such as a test server's.
- `impersonate_service_account` (String) The full name of a service account to act as, `//iam.origincloudapis.eu/organizations/{organization}/serviceAccounts/{service_account}`: the provider exchanges the token of the credentials it found, a person's such as the `origin id login` session, at the security token service for the account's access tokens, and a new one before each expires, so that the plan and apply have the account's roles only. The person needs `iam.service_account.get_access_token` on the account, the role `roles/iam.service-account-token-creator`. The audit log names the service account as the actor and the person as the acting party. A refused exchange fails the plan: the provider never falls back to the person's own token. Left out, `ORIGINCLOUD_IMPERSONATE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT` names the account; set to `""`, the provider impersonates no one, even with the variable set.
- `region` (String) The region whose front door the provider calls, such as `eu-central1`. Every front door serves every resource; a region only picks the nearest. A global service, such as location, is always called at its regionless host. Defaults to `ORIGINCLOUD_REGION`, and to the regionless endpoint when that is unset.
